text: Erasing one bit at room temperature costs at least 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ joules. The floor is not set by silicon or by any manufacturing trick. It is set by counting. A bit has two states; erasing merges them into one, and the merged state holds fewer arrangements than the pair. Entropy drops inside the memory, so it must rise outside it, and it leaves as heat. Rolf Landauer made the argument in 1961: logical irreversibility forces physical irreversibility, at a price of order kT per machine cycle. Here k is the Boltzmann constant and T is the temperature of the memory itself. At 300 K the bill is kT ln 2, which is 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ J for one bit. One joule of waste heat buys 3.5 × 10²⁰ erasures at that floor. Nothing in that sentence mentions a transistor, and nothing in it will need revising when the transistor is gone. Source: Landauer, IBM Journal of Research and Development (1961) · doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183

📡 An object pulsed twice per 62-minute cycle, then went silent for five years In archival MeerKAT data astronomers stumbled on LPT J1555−5631: active for about 15 hours in May 2022, with no pulses or steady emission in five years before or after. The cycle is 62.2 minutes and holds two pulses. The wider main pulse is partly linearly and partly circularly polarized, with a constant polarization angle; the narrow interpulse is almost 100% circularly polarized. They sit 165.4° apart — 14.6° short of exactly opposite. That makes it a near-orthogonal rotator: both magnetic poles show during one rotation, the magnetic axis nearly perpendicular to the spin axis. A constant polarization angle does not fit the standard dipolar polar-cap picture: the magnetosphere is probably broader, the emission coherent — an electron cyclotron maser, perhaps. Neutron star or white dwarf, the data do not settle. Published in ApJ. Plot: Hyman et al. 2026, arXiv:2609.34102 #astronomy #neutronstars @science

🔥 Compound burns fat while sparing muscle UC Berkeley researchers have identified a compound, TOFA, that raises the energy the body spends rather than just curbing appetite. In obese mice it improved blood sugar regulation, cut harmful blood fats, and reduced fat without a significant loss of lean muscle. It also seemed to enhance the effects of weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic when used together. Energy expenditure rose by up to 18%, even though the mice did not move more or warm up. The findings come from mice; safety and effectiveness in humans are not yet established. #obesity #metabolism #UCBerkeley @science

🪞 Google built a fake internet to test its AI agents The Chrome team made the "Mirror Dimension": an isolated copy of the web with thousands of synthetic sites — shops, social feeds, banks. The Auto Browse agent navigates them like the real web; no request leaves the sandbox. The problem: eval awareness — a model notices it is being tested and behaves differently. So the address bar shows the real youtube.com , while underneath headless Chrome runs in a gVisor sandbox and a proxy serves the fake site. To stop the browser flagging the swap, the proxy mints TLS certificates from its own root authority. Agents build the sites too: one writes the spec, another the HTML and CSS, critics check layout via DevTools. Prompt injections are planted in text, images, ARIA labels and tool responses, payload IDs hidden in an HTTP header. The pipeline yields over 1,000 tests per engineer per day, 30× the manual rate. Google published no pass rate, so how well the agent resists is unknown. #AI #security @science

🧠 This model rebuilds what you saw from EEG — and adapts in 15 minutes Alljoined released ENIGMA, which reconstructs a seen image from non-invasive EEG. Accepted at NeurIPS 2025. Pixel-perfect output is impossible: EEG is a mix of millions of neurons' signals through the skull. ENIGMA predicts a CLIP embedding and renders it with SDXL Turbo, so it recovers meaning (sheep, fruit, furniture), not the picture. The real advance is calibration: decoders used to be trained per person for hours, while ENIGMA shares one backbone plus lightweight per-subject layers, so a new user needs ~15 minutes, with under 1% of the previous state of the art's parameters. Tested on Alljoined-1.6M: 20 participants, ~1.6 million trials, a consumer 32-channel Emotiv Flex 2 (~$2,200). Human raters identified the right image from reconstructions in 83.06% of cases on lab-grade data, 65.43% on consumer hardware. Recognition, not mind reading; consumer EEG needs 20+ times the data for lab-grade accuracy. #EEG #BCI @science

One gram of single-stranded DNA can hold 455 exabytes. That is a ceiling set by the molecule, not by an experiment. Four letters, two bits per nucleotide at maximum, so 455 exabytes is 3.6 × 10²¹ bits — and one gram of single-stranded DNA is about 1.8 × 10²¹ nucleotides. The arithmetic closes: this is the density the molecule allows, not something achieved. What was actually written in 2012 was 5.27 megabits — 660 kilobytes — at 5.5 petabits per cubic millimetre, from off-the-shelf DNA. The distance between that and 455 exabytes is synthesis cost and error rate, not physics. 455 exabytes is 455 million one-terabyte drives. And the figure assumes no error-correction overhead: any real archive carries redundancy and lands well below the ceiling. Source: Church, Gao & Kosuri, Science 337, 1628 (2012) · doi.org/10.1126/science.1226355

🧬 Rare disease exposes a hidden immune flaw Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have found that in mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), a rare genetic disorder, natural killer cells fail to mature and cannot properly destroy infected cells. When these cells miss their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, setting off excessive inflammation. The finding, published in Immunity, challenges roughly 30 years of research focused on macrophages. About half of patients do not respond to existing treatments, and the study points to JAK inhibitors as a possible new option. The result is based on blood samples from patients plus preclinical models; no clinical trial has yet tested the new approach. #immunology #genetics #MKD @science

🛰 Voyager 1 crosses one light-day from Earth A light-day is 25.902 billion km — how far light travels in 24 hours. According to JPL Horizons, on 18 November 2026 the probe sits 173.14 AU from Earth (25.901 billion km), with a radio signal taking 23 h 59 min to reach us. It passes the full 24-hour mark on 19 November, around 03:00 UTC. Launched on 5 September 1977, it has flown for almost 49 years. Its speed relative to the Sun is 16.9 km/s, about 3.6 AU per year. The inner edge of the Oort cloud is roughly 300 years away, around 2326; getting out of the cloud will take some 30,000 years. The probe will not leave the galaxy, though: the Oort cloud is still part of the Solar System, and "exit" means only that it clears the outer boundary. #Voyager #space #astronomy @science
